extracted.intended_audience: aspiring screenwriters and writers considering paid script-coverage/listing services
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for screenwriters on how to interpret, use, and evaluate script coverage and numerical scores (e.g., The Black List, Inktip) and whether those services meaningfully advance a screenwriting career.

rubrics_metrics.name: PASS / CONSIDER / RECOMMEND rubric
rubrics_metrics.description: The classic PASS, CONSIDER, and RECOMMEND rubric that has long helped script coverage communicate a script’s commercial or artistic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as the de facto coin of the realm for communicating commercial/artistic value. Historically meaningful and widely used inside studios and among producers. Implication: this binary/ternary evaluation is a useful, industry-proven shorthand for whether a script should move forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical/categorical scoring (plot, character, conflict, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical scoring based on categories such as plot, character, conflict, and other key criteria of a script.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These scores can help a writer or producer gauge progress in the developmental process and guide revisions ("help guide a writer’s next draft"). However, they are subjective, often vary between readers (example: Reader A gives plot 96, Reader B later gives 55), and so should be used as directional feedback rather than absolute truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep coverage/scores private (internal vs public)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scores and coverage are most useful when kept private—akin to internal studio coverage—rather than publicly aggregated on a platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private/internal scores are compared to the public aggregation model of services like The Black List service; the page emphasizes that unlike public listing/aggregation, internal coverage is the only coverage that "really matters." Anti-pattern: posting customers' scores publicly and pitting scripts against each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate curated lists with pay-for services (list vs service)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish The Black List (a hand‑curated published list of the best un‑produced scripts) from The Black List service (a pay-to-play coverage/hosting/scoring service).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page warns that using the same name creates confusion and may mislead writers into thinking they are paying to be on the curated Black List. Advice: verify whether a service is curated by industry contacts or simply a paid hosting/score service before buying in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware implicit marketing promises of industry exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate services for implied promises that industry professionals will discover your script if you buy coverage/hosting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article flags coy/implied marketing language ("industry professionals may discover your script" / "a good score could land you film industry exposure") as misleading. Look past "success stories" and marketing faces; do your own research on actual outcomes and odds before paying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repeat purchases chasing a higher score
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not keep buying one coverage after another in pursuit of a higher score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit advice from the author: they encourage clients to not continually purchase reads to chase a better score. Instead, seek varied free feedback first and then use honest, constructive coverage when needed. Labelled an anti-pattern tied to hope-peddling business models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scores to guide development, not as a contest metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Scores should be used to gauge developmental progress on a script rather than to compare against other scripts or as a marketing weapon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that numerical scores can "genuinely help a writer or producer gauge progress" if treated as internal developmental tools. They criticize platforms that aggregate scores publicly and create competition between customers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize reader variability and subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that different readers may score the same script very differently, reflecting subjectivity in coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given where one reader gives plot 96 and another gives 55. Guidance: treat any single numeric score with caution; look for consistent themes in qualitative feedback rather than fixating on one number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek varied, preferably free, feedback before paying
rubrics_metrics.description: Before purchasing professional coverage, solicit free feedback from writers' groups, cohorts, and peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author encourages using free feedback channels first to improve drafts prior to buying coverage. This reduces wasted spending and reliance on pay-to-play services for developmental notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of 'hope-peddling' business models
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the ethics and value of companies that profit by selling hope—hosting, scoring, and implying industry discovery for paying writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page describes such services as selling "hope and hooey" and warns that as long as pathways into paid screenwriting remain narrow, writers will keep using them. Practical takeaway: do the math on odds vs cost; investigate real success stories before paying; buyer beware.
